sector: B2B SaaS / Data-as-a-Service (Vertical AI for Sales & Marketing)
overview: Black Pearl Group (branded Blackpearl Group) is a Wellington, NZ-headquartered, dual-listed NZX/ASX micro-cap that builds and acquires AI-driven, data-led sales and marketing tools for US small-and-medium businesses (SMBs). Its portfolio spans Pearl Diver (website-visitor identity resolution / buyer-intent lead intelligence), B2B Rocket (AI outbound sales agents, acquired August 2025) and Bebop (an AI sales-intelligence agent launched in 90 days in FY25), all trained on and monetising a proprietary dataset the company calls the 'Pearl Engine' (31bn+ signals/day from 330+ sources) via SaaS subscriptions and an increasingly important Data-as-a-Service (DaaS) offering. Revenue is almost entirely US-dollar SMB spend, reported in NZD, and growth to date has been funded overwhelmingly by repeated equity raises rather than internally generated cash.

business_model.summary: Blackpearl sells subscription access to AI/data products (SaaS) and, increasingly, direct embedded data feeds (DaaS, ~40% of revenue mix by Q1 FY27) to US SMBs and mid-market go-to-market teams, and has begun beta-launching a third layer, Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS), disclosed at the August 2026 AGM. FY26 (year to 31 March 2026) subscription revenue was $13.7m (+77% YoY) against exit ARR of $26.8m (+114% YoY) - a roughly 2x gap between what has been contracted and what has been recognised, which management attributes to ramp-pricing on new DaaS contracts (customers phase up to full billing over ~90 days) and only a partial-year (~7-month, ~40-day-recognised-in-H1) contribution from the newly acquired B2B Rocket. Growth in FY26 was overwhelmingly funded by two equity raises totalling ~$25.3m (a $15.1m placement/ANREO in Aug-2025 at NZ$0.95/share and a further A$10.2m off-market placement in Nov-2025) plus a $5m/$5.27m BNZ debt facility (refinanced to March 2028) - not by operating cash flow, which remains deeply negative. FY26 net loss widened to roughly -$17.8m (EBITDAF loss $15.7m, including $10.2m of one-off acquisition/listing/offer costs) even as revenue grew ~78% YoY to $13.7m.

revenue_streams.name: SaaS subscriptions (Pearl Diver, Bebop, New Old Stamp, B2B Rocket)
revenue_streams.trend: growing but decelerating share as DaaS scales; SaaS churn improved to 4.9% in FY26 (from 5.3% in Q4 FY25) but ticked back up to 5.2% in Q1 FY27

revenue_streams.name: DaaS (embedded data feeds via APIs/partners/MCPs)
revenue_streams.trend: growing fast (~40% of revenue mix by Q1 FY27); FY26 churn reported as 0% for the full year, but the first DaaS customer churn event occurred in Q1 FY27 (~NZ$20k/month ARR) and the contract base is still small ($300k-$700k ARR per client)

business_model.customer_type: B2B, weighted to US SMBs and mid-market sales/marketing teams; top-10 customers were 17% of revenue in FY25 (moderate concentration at the top, but each DaaS deal is individually large relative to total ARR)
business_model.geographic_mix: Predominantly United States end-customers (targeting the ~36 million US SMB market); company headquartered and listed in New Zealand (NZX primary, ASX foreign-exempt dual-listing from Nov-2025), reports in NZD

main_competitors: generalist LLM/agent platforms (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google) increasingly used to build in-house lead-gen and outbound workflows
competitive_position.market_position: Small, sub-scale challenger in a crowded and well-funded B2B data/lead-intelligence category. ARR of $26.8m (FY26) to $27.2m (Q1 FY27) is a rounding error next to ZoomInfo (~US$1.2bn+ revenue) and well-funded private players like Clay and Apollo.io. Management now markets the company explicitly as a 'vertical AI' company - narrower, outcome-trained models sitting 'alongside' rather than competing with foundation-model providers - and in FY26 commissioned a third-party benchmark ('Proto-GTM Bench') claiming the Pearl Engine produces 25x more 'A-grade' commercial records per dollar, at ~1/5th the cost per quality record, versus two unnamed leading generalist/frontier agentic models. The FY26 annual report describes this as a 'third-party' rather than purely self-commissioned benchmark, an upgrade in framing versus FY25/H1, though methodology (five ICP-based tasks, results still labelled 'preliminary', an 'early step' toward a broader benchmark framework) remains narrow and not independently reproducible by outside analysts.

moat_factors.factor: Proprietary outcome data / 'Pearl Engine' ('Moat One: The Data')
moat_factors.description: 31bn signals/day from 330+ sources, over a decade and >NZ$25m of cumulative investment; management argues B2B data decays ~3%/month so continuous refresh beats competitors' periodic updates. Plausible in principle but small in absolute scale next to ZoomInfo's contributor network or Clay's multi-source enrichment waterfall.

moat_factors.factor: Outcome-tuned vertical model ('Moat Two: The Model')
moat_factors.strength: weak-to-moderate, now with third-party benchmark support
moat_factors.description: Management's pitch is that a narrow model trained on real commercial outcomes (not general internet data) beats generalist LLMs on lead-finding tasks - now evidenced by a named third-party 'Proto-GTM Bench' (25x more A-grade records, 5x cheaper per quality record, +18pts output quality vs two unnamed frontier models). Company itself calls this 'early benchmark work' and 'preliminary'; the identity of the benchmarked competitor models is not disclosed, limiting independent verification.

moat_factors.strength: moderate for existing DaaS clients, unproven at scale
moat_factors.description: DaaS clients embed Blackpearl's data directly into revenue workflows via APIs/MCPs, which management argues raises switching costs and explains the reported 0% FY26 churn. DaaS is still new (inception H2 FY25) and the contract base is small ($300k-$700k ARR per client) - the first churn event (Q1 FY27, ~NZ$20k/month) has already occurred as the base has grown.

Limited category recognition versus ZoomInfo or Apollo.io, though B2B Rocket was ranked 45th of 4,664 products in G2's 2026 Best Software Awards (Top Sales Software Products) - a modest but genuine third-party recognition point.

Positioned as materially cheaper than ZoomInfo/Apollo/Kaspr for SMBs - a genuine wedge into the price-sensitive SMB segment - but commoditisation pressure from LLM-native tools (Clay, Common Room, generic agent frameworks SMBs can now assemble themselves) is compressing this advantage from the low end.

No meaningful regulatory moat; data-privacy compliance (fair use of scraped/enriched contact data, CAN-SPAM, GDPR/CCPA-adjacent rules) is a shared cost of doing business across the category, not a Blackpearl-specific advantage.

weaknesses: Sub-scale versus well-capitalised, VC-backed or public competitors (ZoomInfo, Apollo.io, Clay) with far larger data assets and marketing budgets
Core moat claim, while now attributed to a named third-party benchmark, still rests on a single, preliminary study against two unnamed competitor models rather than broad independent verification
DaaS 'near-zero churn' track record is short (about 2 years) and built on a small number of large contracts, making it highly sensitive to a single logo loss - which has already begun (Q1 FY27 churn)

Product line is an assembled portfolio of small/bolt-on acquisitions (New Old Stamp, B2B Rocket) rather than one deeply integrated platform, raising execution/integration risk, though management cites B2B Rocket integration synergies as evidence this can be managed

Structurally exposed to LLM commoditisation: as frontier models get cheaper and better at exactly the lead-finding/enrichment tasks Blackpearl sells, the addressable premium for a smaller vertical player narrows
Continuing to add a third product layer (Platform-as-a-Service, beta launched mid-2026) while still not cash-flow positive on the first two layers raises execution-focus risk

growth_drivers: DaaS scale-out: management guides to DaaS continuing to grow as a share of the mix (already ~40% of revenue by Q1 FY27), with deeper embedding, higher per-contract ARR ($300k-$700k) and structurally lower churn than SaaS

New Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS) layer: early beta launched by mid-2026, described by management as 'the next evolution' of the business model and a new revenue opportunity layered on top of SaaS and DaaS

B2B Rocket cross-sell and full-year contribution: only a partial year was recognised in FY26 (acquired August 2025), so FY27 subscription revenue should mechanically catch up toward the ARR run-rate; management cites $1.8m of annualised FY27 cost synergies against a $0.5m integration cost

Compressing the ARR-to-revenue timing lag via the explicit 'five levers' plan for FY27: shorter DaaS ramp cycles, tighter ideal-customer-profile (ICP) targeting, post-acquisition cost optimisation, improved cash collection, and fixed-cost infrastructure leverage

Gross margin operating leverage: data supply agreements moved from variable to a fixed annual cost structure during FY26 (crossover complete), so as revenue scales without a matching cost increase, gross margin should mechanically expand (68.6% FY26, guided higher in FY27)
Stated path to $50m ARR within 3-5 years; ARR already at $27.2m at Q1 FY27, above the $26.8m FY26 year-end figure

Sequential EBITDAF loss narrowing already evidenced: Q1 FY27 loss of $4.5m, with guidance for $2.5-3.0m (Q2 FY27) and $1.0-1.5m (Q3 FY27) - if delivered, the first real evidence that scale is translating into cash discipline

business.description: $26.8m FY26 ARR vs $13.7m recognised subscription revenue is roughly a 2x gap. Management attributes this to ramp pricing and partial-period acquisition contribution and has laid out a specific 'five levers' plan to close it in FY27, but a persistent, widening gap between headline ARR and cash-generating revenue remains the metric investors should be most skeptical of in a story stock.

DaaS contracts run $300k-$700k in ARR each, implying a relatively small number of relationships underpin a large and growing share of ARR (~40% of revenue by Q1 FY27). The heavily marketed 'zero churn' claim for FY26 is a small-sample, short-history statistic that had already broken by Q1 FY27 (one DaaS customer churned, ~NZ$20k/month ARR). Further DaaS losses would materially dent both ARR growth and the 'sticky data embedding' narrative.

The Group now runs three applications (Pearl Diver, B2B Rocket, Bebop) across three monetisation layers (SaaS, DaaS, and an emerging PaaS beta) - increasing execution and integration complexity while the core business has not yet reached cash breakeven.

financial.description: FY26 EBITDAF loss was $15.7m (including $10.2m of one-off acquisition/listing/offer costs) and the reported net loss widened to roughly -$17.8m even as revenue grew ~78% YoY. H1 FY26 alone saw a net free cash outflow (ex the B2B Rocket acquisition) of $7.1m in six months. Cash was $9.6m at 31 March 2026. The company has layered $5.27m of BNZ debt (refinanced to March 2028) on top of two equity raises totalling ~$25.3m in FY26 alone - a pattern of continuous external funding, not self-sufficiency, even as guided EBITDAF losses are set to narrow through FY27.

Both FY26 capital raises (the Aug-2025 $15.1m placement/ANREO at NZ$0.95/share, and the Nov-2025 A$10.2m off-market placement of 11.8m shares, ratified at the Aug-2026 AGM) were priced well below the Nov-2024 peak of ~$1.39 and each added meaningfully to the share count. The Board explicitly sought and received AGM approval (Aug-2026) for continued 'flexibility to issue further equity quickly for future growth opportunities,' signalling further dilutive raises remain a live possibility unless the FY27 loss-narrowing trajectory (guided Q3 FY27 EBITDAF loss of $1.0-1.5m) is delivered.

$5.27m of BNZ borrowings (refinanced to March 2028, subject to continued covenant compliance) sit on a balance sheet with persistent operating losses; covenant or refinancing risk rises if losses do not narrow as guided.

Revenue is overwhelmingly USD-denominated (US SMB customers) while the company reports in NZD and is NZX/ASX-listed (one raise was even denominated in AUD); NZD/USD and AUD/NZD moves create translation noise in reported growth rates.

regulatory.description: The core product is built on scraped/enriched B2B contact and behavioural data; tightening US state privacy laws, CAN-SPAM-style enforcement, or platform-level restrictions (e.g., LinkedIn/email providers clamping down on outbound automation and enrichment) could raise compliance costs or restrict data sourcing for Pearl Diver, B2B Rocket and DaaS alike.

ASX foreign-exempt dual-listing (completed Nov-2025) adds ongoing compliance and reporting costs; $1.2m of FY26's one-off costs were directly attributed to ASX listing and associated expenses. The company also does not fully comply with several NZX Corporate Governance Code recommendations (e.g., independent chair, 20-working-day AGM notice in 2025) given its size.

macro.description: Customer base is US SMBs, a discretionary-spend cohort typically first to cut software/marketing spend in a slowdown; CAC payback improved to 3.5 months by Q4 FY26 (best-in-class per Bessemer benchmarks) but had lengthened to 6.3 months by Q1 FY27, which management frames as a deliberate trade for transition rather than demand weakening.

Market cap around NZ$40-45m with thin daily turnover. Small-cap, loss-making, story-stock names are typically first sold in a risk-off environment; illiquidity itself widens the range of plausible fair prices. Shares were down roughly 53% year-to-date and well below the Nov-2024 peak of ~$1.39 as of late FY27 reporting.

macro.risk: LLM commoditisation of the core product category
macro.description: General-purpose LLMs and agent frameworks are rapidly improving at exactly the lead-finding/enrichment/outreach tasks Blackpearl monetises. Even with a favourable third-party benchmark today, if frontier models close part of the quality gap, the pricing premium and differentiation for a small vertical player erodes quickly - a structural threat larger, better-capitalised competitors (ZoomInfo, Apollo, Clay) are also racing to address, but from a position of far greater data scale and R&D budget.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: B2B sales intelligence / data-as-a-service is a large, growing category (driven by AI-enabled outbound and account-based marketing, and roughly US$600bn of committed global AI infrastructure investment per Stanford HAI's 2026 AI Index cited by the company) but is also rapidly commoditising as LLMs absorb enrichment and lead-scoring workflows that used to require dedicated vendors. Growth is real across the sector, but competitive intensity and price pressure are both rising simultaneously; 'vertical AI' (domain-specific models wrapped around foundation models) is the framing management and, per its own commentary, capital markets are increasingly rewarding.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate-to-high - reliant on US SMB marketing/sales tooling budgets, which are among the more discretionary and cyclical categories of software spend.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High indirectly: as an unprofitable, cash-burning micro-cap reliant on repeated equity/debt raises to fund growth, higher rates and risk-off conditions directly raise its cost/availability of capital and depress the multiple the market will pay for ARR growth.
key_input_costs: Third-party/underlying data supply agreements (now fixed-cost annual contracts as of FY26)
Cloud/compute costs for the Pearl Engine and LLM-adjacent infrastructure
US sales & marketing headcount (SMB go-to-market is labour- and CAC-intensive)

recent_developments.event: Completed acquisition of US-based B2B Rocket Inc. (AI outbound sales automation) for US$4m cash plus 1.725m BPG shares (21 Aug 2025); launched and completed an oversubscribed $15.1m capital raise (institutional placement + accelerated non-renounceable entitlement offer) at a fixed price of NZ$0.95/share

H1 FY26 result: ARR $19.5m (+87% YoY), subscription revenue $5.2m (+59% YoY), gross margin compressed to 67% (crossover between variable and fixed data-supply agreements), CAC payback 4.6 months (+34% YoY)
Completed a further A$10.2m off-market placement of 11.8m shares, broadening the institutional shareholder base (including new Australian institutions) ahead of the ASX dual-listing
Completed dual (foreign-exempt) listing on the ASX alongside the existing NZX listing

FY26 (year to 31 March 2026) full-year result: record ARR $26.8m (+114% YoY), subscription revenue $13.7m (+77% YoY, ~78% cited elsewhere), gross margin 68.6% (up from 67.8% FY25), EBITDAF loss $15.7m (including $10.2m of one-off acquisition/listing/offer costs), net loss widened to approximately -$17.8m, cash $9.6m, BNZ facility refinanced to $5m/March 2028; management laid out a 'five levers' plan to compress the ARR-to-revenue timing lag and elevate cash conversion to an equal priority alongside ARR growth in FY27

Q1 FY27 trading update (28 July 2026): ARR $27.2m (+95% YoY, +2% sequential), EBITDAF loss $4.5m, guidance for losses to narrow to $2.5-3.0m (Q2 FY27) and $1.0-1.5m (Q3 FY27); SaaS churn ticked up to 5.2%; CAC payback lengthened to 6.3 months (from 3.5 months at Q4 FY26); DaaS now ~40% of revenue mix but recorded its first customer churn (~NZ$20k/month ARR); disclosed early beta launch of a new Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS) offering; new benchmark cited the Pearl Engine scoring 26x the leading foundational model without proprietary data access and 6.6x with it

Held 2026 Annual Shareholders' Meeting (5 Aug, virtual); shareholders ratified the November 2025 A$10.2m/11.8m-share placement and approved continued board flexibility to issue further equity for growth opportunities; B2B Rocket ranked 45th of 4,664 products in G2's 2026 Best Software Awards (Top Sales Software Products)

Shares trading in the roughly NZ$0.50-0.66 range (multiple sources cite different recent closes), down materially from the Nov-2024 peak of ~$1.39 and down roughly 53% year-to-date in 2026 (market cap approximately NZ$40-45m) despite record ARR growth - reflecting market skepticism on cash burn, dilution, the ARR-to-revenue conversion lag, and DaaS concentration rather than any single negative catalyst identified in company announcements

guidance.as_of: Q1 FY27 trading update (28 July 2026) and FY26 results / Annual Report (May 2026)

items.vs_prior: reiterated from the FY26 result's initial framing
items.notes: Implies roughly 70-80% sequential loss narrowing from Q1 FY27's $4.5m loss to the Q3 midpoint; delivery is the key swing factor for whether further dilutive capital raises are needed
ARR was $26.8m at FY26-end and $27.2m at Q1 FY27 (+2% sequential); the $30m ARR milestone was described by management as 'fast approaching' as of the FY26 result
Driven mechanically by the now-completed shift to fixed (from variable) data-supply-agreement cost structure as revenue scales

items.target: Elevated to an equal-weighted priority alongside ARR growth via five specific FY27 levers (shorter DaaS ramps, tighter ICP, post-acquisition cost optimisation, improved cash collection, fixed-cost infrastructure leverage)
items.vs_prior: new emphasis - explicit shift from FY26's growth-at-all-costs framing
items.notes: Management states the FY26 one-off costs ($10.2m) are 'behind' the business and all five levers are 'in motion' as of the FY26 result

items.target: $1.8m annualised FY27 cost savings against a $0.5m integration cost (3.6x payback)
items.notes: Structural, described by management as permanent rather than cyclical cost reductions from eliminating duplicate customer success/operational functions

guidance.management_commentary: FY26 result commentary: 'The $10.2 million in one-off non-recurring costs in FY26 are now behind us... Five specific levers are now in motion - each directly converting contracted ARR into recognised revenue and cash.' CEO Nick Lissette: 'FY26 proved the model works. FY27 is about showing what that model can return.' Q1 FY27 update frames the lengthened CAC payback (3.5 to 6.3 months) as 'a deliberate trade for transition' rather than demand-side weakening, and continues to describe DaaS as a 'validated,' low-churn, compounding revenue stream despite the first DaaS churn event occurring in the same quarter. At the August 2026 AGM, management outlined evolution of the revenue model across SaaS, DaaS, and a newly disclosed Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS) layer, alongside continued emphasis on reaching EBITDAF profitability.

bull_case: FY26 ARR growth of 114% YoY and Q1 FY27 ARR of $27.2m (+95% YoY) is genuinely rapid top-line momentum, and if the guided Q1-to-Q3 FY27 EBITDAF loss narrowing (roughly $4.5m to $1.0-1.5m) is delivered, the business could approach breakeven without further heavily dilutive raises
Gross margin structurally improving (67.8% to 68.6%, guided higher) as data-supply costs have now fully shifted from variable to fixed - a genuine operating-leverage mechanism, not just a promise

DaaS and the newly disclosed Platform-as-a-Service layer represent real product innovation for the category - embedding data directly into a customer's revenue workflow plausibly does raise switching costs versus a standalone SaaS seat, and even a moderated (non-zero) churn rate could make DaaS/PaaS a materially better business than pure SaaS lead-gen tools

The FY26 third-party 'Proto-GTM Bench' benchmark, while preliminary and against unnamed competitors, is an incremental improvement in evidentiary support for the company's core moat claim versus purely self-commissioned marketing in prior years

The stock's roughly 53% YTD decline in 2026 and its distance from the Nov-2024 peak (~$1.39) already discount significant execution risk; if FY27 guidance is met, the stock is starting from a low valuation base relative to $26.8m+ of ARR and a $50m medium-term ARR target

B2B Rocket's full-year contribution (only a partial period recognised in FY26 following the August 2025 acquisition) has not yet fully flowed through the P&L, so FY27 subscription revenue should mechanically catch up toward the ARR run-rate even without further sales execution
bear_case: Successive equity raises priced below prior peaks (NZ$0.95/share Aug-2025, further placement Nov-2025) have diluted shareholders materially, and FY26 cash burn (EBITDAF loss $15.7m, net loss widened to roughly -$17.8m) makes further dilution likely unless the FY27 loss-narrowing guidance is met precisely; the Board explicitly sought and received renewed authority at the Aug-2026 AGM to issue more equity quickly

The roughly 2x gap between $26.8m ARR and $13.7m recognised subscription revenue is not fully explained by ramp timing alone and deserves scrutiny as a metric-quality issue; ARR is a forward-looking, non-audited KPI the company itself defines, while recognised revenue is the audited, cash-relevant number

The headline 'zero/near-zero DaaS churn' claim, built on a small number ($300k-$700k ARR each) of contracts over roughly a two-year history, already broke in Q1 FY27 with the first DaaS customer loss - undermining the core 'sticky, self-reinforcing' investment thesis management has built around DaaS

The claimed moat (a 25x-better proprietary 'Pearl Engine') rests on a single, preliminary benchmark against unnamed competitor models in a category (B2B contact data/lead intelligence) dominated by far larger, better-capitalised incumbents (ZoomInfo, Apollo.io) and fast-moving, well-funded challengers (Clay, Common Room) - all facing the same LLM-commoditisation pressure Blackpearl does, but from a stronger data and capital position

NZX/ASX micro-cap illiquidity (market cap ~NZ$40-45m, thin daily turnover) means the stock can re-rate sharply on thin volume in either direction, and a loss-making, dilution-dependent story stock is typically among the first sold in a risk-off market - which is at least as parsimonious an explanation for the sustained share-price decline as any single fundamental catalyst identified in company disclosures to date

Management is now layering a third monetisation model (Platform-as-a-Service, beta) onto a business that has not yet demonstrated it can convert its existing SaaS/DaaS ARR into cash profitably, raising the risk of diluted management focus during a critical 'growth to cash' transition year
